summary: A status update from BBN on the troubled release of IMPSYS 2600. It recaps the attempts on May 15, May 31 and June 6, where the TIP version failed badly and the old systems were put back. It reports on later efforts to get the new system running.

plainLanguage.summary: The people running the network keep trying to switch to new software and keep having to switch back. This note is a diary of the tries so far.

subtitle: A June 1972 progress report on repeated attempts to switch the ARPANET to the new IMP system, release 2600.

tldr.problem: The network operators wanted to replace the old IMP software with a new system (2600) at more than twenty-five sites, and users needed to know where that stood.
tldr.mechanism: The note recaps each trial date and why it was abandoned, then lists the planned dates for the next tries.
tldr.outcome: As of June 22, 1972 the new system was still not up. It obsoletes RFC 343.

today: This is a dated status note that obsoletes RFC 343. It describes the situation on 22 June 1972 only.

sections.title: Still Not Up
sections.content:
Dave Walden of BBN opens with a blunt headline: the new IMP system (2600) is still not up. The RFC is dated 22 June 1972, is marked Category B.1 and obsoletes RFC 343.

The text recaps what has been tried so far and says what comes next.
sections.plainLanguage: The message starts by saying the new software is still not working on the network.

sections.title: The Failed Attempts
sections.content:
The RFC lists four tries:

  • May 15: the team badly underestimated the difficulty of distributing the system to over twenty-five sites and never got around to debugging it.
  • May 31: with a distribution mechanism in place, they debugged the system but found problems that prevented leaving it up.
  • June 6: the new IMP system worked quite well, but the matching TIP system hardly worked at all, so the old systems went back up.
  • June 20: IMPs and TIPs loaded and flew well and were left up, but by the afternoon of June 21 TIPs were crashing about once an hour, so the old systems were restored.
sections.plainLanguage: They tried four times. First it was too hard to hand out the new software, then it had bugs, then one half did not work, and finally things kept crashing every hour.

sections.title: The Plan for Next Tries
sections.content:
The author plans to skip Tuesday, June 27, and Tuesday, July 4, and to try again on Thursday, July 6 (1972). If needed, the next try is Tuesday, July 18, and following Tuesdays, as set out in RFC 343.

The note explains why TIP crashes hurt so much: one crash per hour across the network means roughly one crash every eight or ten hours when debugging with a single TIP, which makes the bug hunt nasty.
sections.plainLanguage: They will wait a few weeks and try again on a set day. Finding bugs is slow because a crash only shows up on one machine every eight or ten hours.
